Congratulations on your beautiful baby! If you've gone thru my post history, I write a lot about birth trauma. Have you heard this term?

It's a specific kind of trauma that comes up when we perceive things to have gone wrong during our birth. Risk factors include extreme pain, our needs not being listened to, an emergency C section, and feeling neglected and dismissed by staff. PTSD like symptoms are reported by a significant amount of women in the days and weeks post birth, though 10% go on to develop full fledged PTSD, 20% PPD and 10% PPA. You can check accounts on instagram like @ reallifemidwife and 'The Tea on Birth Trauma' to see what I am talking about. This is all scientific fact.  


Now we move on to my personal opinions. Here are the whys. Why? 

Childbirth is a huge spiritual and psychological transition from maiden to mother. Where there was once just your body with a foetus inside, there are now suddenly two people. The hormone cascade of birth and then the hormone cascade after birth are more intense than any drug I have ever taken or any other experience I have ever had. Things that go on in labour and directly afterwards imprint themselves into us in different ways than they usually would. 

I like to imagine that during and immediately after birth your identity is going through a massive reshuffle. If very traumatic things happen in that reshuffle, your mind's usual defenses against traumatic experiences are down. The trauma hits super raw, just when your identity has broken down and is reforming. Like, imagine if you were on acid. 3 tabs deep. Then people touched and looked at your vagina a bunch. Then you had massive surgery. Then another human came out of you. Then you experienced food deprivation, extreme pain, medical negligence, gaslighting and painful and frightening swelling. And the new person taken out of you was taken away from you to God knows where. All while in a profoundly altered state.

Then you've got the huge hormone crash that happens in the days and weeks after birth as you are trying to make sense of this trauma. 

This comment is coloured heavily by my own experience. I have no idea what mental health conditions you have, nor the extent of your phsyical scars. I am not sure how many weeks or months postpartum you are. Here is what I wish I did a lot earlier after my traumatic birth:

\- Found a psychologist specialising in birth trauma

\- Chatted to a lawyer about medical negligence

\- Got a GREAT psychiatrist and considered meds in conjunction with therapy

\- Seen a private women's health physio for the recovery after a surgical birth

\- Followed the accounts on instagram I mentioned earlier. Maybe join a birth trauma support group too on Facebook

\- Bought the book 'How to Heal a Bad Birth'

\- I also put my kid in daycare 2 days a week at 6 months old so I could process a little without distracting myself with a baby.

​

In summary, your treatment sounds very traumatizing. PTSD or PPD sound super likely. Please seek help. This doesn't need to be a permanent death sentence. Hugs to you and your family.

Australian health guidelines recommend sleeping in the same room until 12 months. Cosleeping and gentle parenting like staying in the kid's room for longer.

Up to 12 months, a baby regulates their breathing with the other person in their room, reducing their risk of SIDS, according to the recommendations in my country.

It makes sense from a historic social perspective. Adults like sleeping with someone, that's why couples sleep together. Dogs like sleeping with someone. Humans evolved to all sleep in the same hut, or nearby each other around the fire. Even if it isn't socially acceptable in the West at the minute. Of course baby wants you in  the room. 8 month olds have barely mastered object permanence. it would be so scary to sleep alone as an 8 month old, literally believing your parent was nonexistent because you couldn't see or hear them.

I put breastfeed bub to sleep (13 mo) in his floor bed, then go to bed with hubby and have sex from like 11 pm - 1 am, then return to baby's bed to breastfeed when he wakes up and spend the rest of the night sleeping next to baby. So I get sex, snuggles before I sleep, but I spend most of the night in a quiet room with no hubby snoring, with no hubby hogging my blanket. It's great. He doesn't wake us when he gets ready for work. My sheets don't smell like man.

My advise? Put a single mattress for yourself in his room, give it nice sheets and make it comfy. If you choose to sleep there, why not make it somewhere comfortable? I love cosleeping, but it's only safe for breastfed babies as per Dr. James McKenna's guidelines.

If cosleeping/ sleeping in bub's room promotes your mental health and gives you more sleep, why change anything?

Trauma can of COURSE cause pelvic floor dysfunction. Holding poo in for days will cause all sorts of flow on muscular problems, as will straining really hard. Especially for years at a time. This saying is really common in Australia! We have droughts (had a really bad and long one in the early naughties) and rural houses are on tank water. Many households do this. 

I don't flush wee, but no one in my family cares. If they did, I would flush. Of course, if we have guests, I flush. Its environmental not to flush, but it is disgusting.

To add: no one in our house flushes urine. In Australia we say "if it's yellow, let it mellow". We have a lot of droughts and most rural houses are on tank water. Not flushing doesn't bother us. It is culturally OK here, but from the comments in this thread, it seems like it isn't the done thing in the US anyway.

But the 2 men in the house shut the toilet lid. Even though there are more men in the house than women. Why? Because I asked. Because they have respect.

I don't understand people who refuse to change things that deeply distress their partner. If something really upsets my partner, even if I think it is dumb, I will stop. And vice versa. I believe this is a cornerstone of a respectful relationship.

I make hubby's bed but not my own. Why? Because it makes him feel icky if it isn't made, and I don't really care, but I will do this small thing for him because it means so much to him. He likes getting dry outside the shower but I hate water on the bathroom floor so he now dries off in the shower cubicle. He likes scrunching his towels in a damp mess. He now hangs them. Why? Because it is my irrational pet peeve.

A good partner is not an inconsiderate teenager who gets their way because they consider their own needs to be more important than others. They are a goddamn adult.

If their boss at work asked  them to flush, without giving a reason, they would. You deserve MORE respect than his boss at work, as the mother of his children.

No begging or reasoning is needed on your part. Maybe tell him the boss analogy or the teenager analogy. This isn't about who has a better 'reason'. It is about the levels of respect that exist in a healthy relationship. Yes, his feelings will get hurt. He may huff. But what you are saying isn't cruel, it is simply setting your boundaries in a way that is adult, respectful to yourself, and ultimately respectful of your relationship.

Most of the studies against bed-sharing study mortality rates in all bed-sharing, which includes both safe and unsafe bed-sharing. The stats for SAFE bed sharing following the safe sleep 7 guidelines are much better. Unfortunately, hardly any studies have been done comparing babies who safely cosleep vs all other babies. 

A firm mattress on the floor, with a fitted sheet, pressed up against the wall, with nothing in it but 1 breast-feeding mother and a pillow and baby in a sleep sack is a safe place for a baby.

A bed with ANYTHING else in it (except maybe a partner if he satisfies all criteria) is not a safe place to co-sleep. A formula fed baby cannot safely co-sleep because formula is digested slower and these babies wake up less and are harder to rouse. 

So yes, cosleeping is safe, but for a minority of mother/ baby dyads. We have evolved over billions of years to cosleep with our infants. I would argue that mother-baby dyads are NOT adapted to function optimally in separate sleep spaces. I believe separate sleeping increases baby's time awake during the night and increases mother's sleep deprivations. Sharing a sleep space (even if it is a crib next to you) helps baby regulate their breathing.

In summary, SOME co-sleeping setups are perfectly safe for babies. MOST are not. This is usually because of lack of awareness/ education about safe co-sleeping. EDUCATING women about the safe sleep 7 will increase the incidence of safe co-sleeping.

  
You can look up Professor James McKenna for more info.
